prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a mid-size passenger airline based in Mexico D.F. The airline operates on the Hub & Spoke model and is seeking to increase its revenue. It intends to do so by switching the only airplane currently serving the flight to Mango, Brazil (an agricultural outpost) to their existing New York line service.
prompt.question: Is switching the Mango, Brazil plane to the New York line a good idea? Will it increase revenue?

clarifying_info.q: What type of airplane serves the Brazil line?
How many flights does the Brazil plane make?
clarifying_info.a: It makes two round trips a day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the occupancy rate on the Brazil line?
What does a round trip ticket to Brazil cost?
How many planes currently serve the New York line?
clarifying_info.a: 4 planes, each similar to the Brazil plane (200 seats).

clarifying_info.q: How many round trips do the New York planes make?
clarifying_info.a: Each makes 3 round trips a day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the occupancy rate on the New York line?
What is the ticket price on the New York line?
What would happen to occupancy if a fifth plane is added to NY?
clarifying_info.a: The occupancy rate would drop to 70%.

framework: Clarify that costs are not relevant — focus purely on revenue
Calculate current total revenue: Brazil line + New York line
Calculate new total revenue if the Brazil plane is moved to the NY line (5 NY planes at reduced occupancy, Brazil eliminated)
Compare current vs. new revenue to determine if the switch increases or decreases revenue
Assess qualitative factors: impact on demand for Brazil/South America routes, customer satisfaction, and strategic network effects

questions.prompt: What is the current revenue from the Brazil (Mango) line?
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply seats × round trips per day × occupancy rate × ticket price. Both legs of a round trip count as two one-way trips, so one round trip ticket = 2 passenger-seat movements, but the standard approach here is: revenue per day = seats × trips × occupancy × ticket price (where ticket price is round trip).

math.setup: Brazil daily revenue = seats × round trips per day × occupancy rate × round-trip ticket price
steps: 200 seats × 2 round trips × 0.90 occupancy × $350 per round trip

questions.prompt: What is the current revenue from the New York line?
questions.guidance: Same formula applied to 4 planes each making 3 round trips at 80% occupancy.

math.setup: NY daily revenue = seats × round trips per day per plane × number of planes × occupancy rate × round-trip ticket price

questions.prompt: What is the current combined (total) revenue?
questions.guidance: Sum of Brazil and NY lines.

math.setup: Total current revenue = Brazil revenue + NY revenue

questions.prompt: What would the new revenue be if the Brazil plane is moved to New York (5 NY planes, Brazil line eliminated)?
questions.guidance: NY now has 5 planes, each making 3 round trips, but occupancy drops to 70%. Brazil revenue disappears entirely.

math.setup: New NY daily revenue = seats × round trips per day per plane × number of planes × new occupancy rate × ticket price

questions.prompt: Does the switch increase or decrease revenue, and by how much?
questions.guidance: Compare new vs. current total revenue.

math.setup: Revenue change = New revenue − Current revenue

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the revenue calculation, what other factors or repercussions should the CEO consider before eliminating the Mango route?

categories.name: Network and Demand Effects
ideas: Removing Mango service may reduce feeder traffic connecting to other South American routes
Customers traveling to/from Mango may switch entirely to a competitor, weakening the airline's South American presence
Hub & Spoke dynamics: losing a spoke can reduce hub utilization

categories.name: Customer and Brand Impact
ideas: Unsatisfied Mango customers may leave negative reviews and damage brand reputation
Business travelers relying on the route may switch loyalty programs
The agricultural outpost may have time-sensitive cargo or seasonal demand that generates premium pricing

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: A competitor could quickly fill the Mango route void and gain a foothold
Mango route may have regulatory or bilateral air-rights requirements that are hard to reclaim once surrendered

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: Adding a 5th plane to NY may require additional gate slots, crew, or maintenance that introduce costs
Existing NY overcapacity signals demand is not strong enough to absorb more supply

categories.name: Revenue Quality
ideas: The Brazil line's 90% occupancy vs. NY's projected 70% shows Brazil is more efficiently loaded
High load factor on Brazil suggests unmet demand; the route may have pricing upside instead

recommendation: Do NOT switch the Brazil plane to New York — the move would decrease daily revenue by $63,000 (from $798k to $735k)
The Mango/Brazil route is highly profitable on a per-seat basis (90% load factor) and should be retained
If revenue growth is the goal, explore raising Brazil ticket prices, adding capacity on the Brazil route if demand supports it, or finding ways to improve NY load factors before adding more capacity
risks: Adding a 5th NY plane and losing Brazil route eliminates a high-load route while over-supplying a lower-demand market
Abandoning the Mango route risks permanently losing those customers and any connected South American network value
next_steps: Analyze whether Brazil ticket prices can be raised given the 90% occupancy (pricing power test)
Investigate why NY occupancy is only 80% — is it a pricing, scheduling, or demand issue?
Evaluate whether the airline could add flights on both routes by sourcing an additional aircraft rather than cannibalizing an existing route
